news.title: Anthropic launches Claude Sheets, Meetings and Whiteboards
news.summary: Anthropic unveiled a spreadsheet tool in beta, a meeting participant for Google Meet and a whiteboard organizer, and made Claude Data and Interactive Connectors generally available. Coverage tied a 2.2% dip in Microsoft shares to the office-suite push.

news.title: Google makes Gemini 4 Carbon available on its API and AI Ultra
news.summary: Gemini 4 Carbon, Google's model for long-running coding, cybersecurity and scientific reasoning, is now open to paid API and AI Ultra users at introductory pricing that rises after November 30. It leads several agent benchmarks, including CursorBench.

news.title: Anthropic sets its IPO price range at $70 to $78 a share
news.summary: Anthropic launched its roadshow with 825 million Class A shares to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, a day after earlier pricing details were pulled. Reports say Nvidia and Google each plan to buy about $10B of stock.

news.title: DeepMind's AlphaProof Code formally verifies parts of Signal's protocol
news.summary: An agentic system wrote about 6.5 million lines of machine-checked Lean proofs covering Signal's PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet code in roughly four weeks. DeepMind open-sourced the proofs and framework.

news.title: OpenAI's third-quarter operating loss reaches $10.9B
news.summary: Investor documents seen by the Journal show OpenAI's quarterly revenue rose about 50% to around $10B, but the operating loss widened even as its margin improved.

news.title: Mercor raises $750M at a $20B valuation
news.summary: The AI training company, which uses a network of over five million experts to evaluate and post-train frontier models, raised a Series D with Nvidia, Salesforce and Zoom among participants. It plans to spend on evaluations, post-training and more agent training environments.

news.title: Nvidia shareholders sue over undisclosed Huang ties to alleged spy
news.summary: A securities class action in San Jose accuses Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang of hiding a relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a firm linked to alleged Chinese espionage. Nvidia stock fell about 5 to 6% on the day.

news.title: IBM and Microsoft launch an industry agent platform with 6,000 prebuilt agents
news.summary: The jointly built Imagine Enterprise platform bundles industry-specific agents with governance controls that log agent actions and enforce limits on how much they can do on their own.

news.title: Google Cloud previews Gemini for Healthcare with seven hospital customers
news.summary: The US preview agent reads electronic health records through read-only access to prepare patient charts and prior-authorization packets, with Northwell among the launch partners.

news.title: OpenAI opens Businesses in ChatGPT in beta
news.summary: Verified companies can claim profiles inside ChatGPT and deploy agents that answer product questions, starting with eligible US e-commerce and online-service firms. Sponsored agents can also serve as ad destinations.

news.title: Meituan releases open weights for its 1.6T-parameter LongCat-2.5
news.summary: The Chinese delivery giant published its mixture-of-experts agent model with vision and a 1-million-token context window under the permissive MIT license.

news.title: Railway breach runs up about $740K in fraudulent AI charges
news.summary: Attackers used two zero-day flaws in the cloud platform to steal customers' AI provider keys and rack up usage. Railway says it will cover charges that providers decline to refund.

papers.title: From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings
papers.tldr: A new benchmark shows frontier AI agents rarely ask the questions that would change their plans, producing infeasible first plans on 58–98% of tasks when details are missing.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper builds a test called Ask2Decide that checks whether AI agents ask people the right questions before making a plan, and finds that today's best models mostly don't.

## Background you need
An LLM agent is a language model that takes actions, such as drafting a delivery schedule, for a person. Real requests are often missing details, so a good agent should ask. Here, "decision-relevant" facts are ones that would change the best plan; "twins" are facts that sound similar but don't matter.

## The problem
Most agent tests hand the model every fact up front. Others use AI-simulated users that answer too helpfully. Real people are vague and short in their replies. So agents may look capable in tests but build wrong plans in practice, for example a route plan that ignores a closed road nobody mentioned.

## The idea
Think of a good contractor before a kitchen remodel. They don't ask about your favorite color of screws. They ask about the load-bearing wall and the plumbing, because those change the plan. Ask2Decide measures whether an agent acts like that contractor: asking about facts that matter and skipping look-alike details that don't.

## How it works
1. **Planning tasks with gaps.** The benchmark has 43 planning problems, drawn from standard operations-research collections like vehicle routing and scheduling. The agent gets a short brief and an incomplete set of notes.
2. **A human-like "operator."** An operator holds the hidden facts. The agent can send up to 15 messages to ask before submitting its first plan.
3. **Math decides what matters.** Optimization solvers (exact problem-solving software) compute how much each hidden fact changes the best plan. Each important fact is paired with a similar-sounding twin that changes nothing.
4. **A study with real people.** Nineteen people played the operator across 79 sessions. After a wrong plan, people left out the correcting fact 43% of the time, versus 7% for a default AI operator.
5. **A calibrated simulator.** The authors built CalOp, an AI operator tuned to match those human habits, so the test reflects how real users reply.

## Results
The team tested four frontier models: GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM-5.3 Flash. When they had to ask for information, their first plans were infeasible (broke a real constraint) on 58 to 98% of tasks. When given every fact up front, that dropped to 5 to 28%. So the hard part is gathering information, not planning.

Agents uncovered 39 to 52% of the facts that mattered, but also 32 to 41% of the irrelevant twins. In other words, they barely tell useful questions from noise. Some models rarely asked at all: GLM-5.3 Flash averaged 0.6 questions per task. Asking a lot didn't guarantee success either. On the hardest tier, GPT-6.1 Sol asked 11.2 questions per task but learned only 37% of the relevant facts.

CalOp's behavior was much closer to real people than the default simulator. Its distance score from human behavior was 0.213, versus 0.395.

## Why it matters
Assistants that book trips, plan logistics or schedule staff will face missing details every day. This benchmark shows where they fail, and gives builders a way to train and measure better question-asking. The human-calibrated operator also offers a fairer way to test other interactive agents.

## Caveats
The human study is small: 19 people on 22 tasks. The simulator comparison used one model and one random seed. Some labels come from an AI judge, not humans. The authors note the work is ongoing and will be updated.

## Key terms
- **LLM agent:** a language model that plans or acts on someone's behalf.
- **Operator:** the person, or simulated person, who knows the hidden facts.
- **Infeasible plan:** a plan that breaks at least one real-world rule or limit.
- **Twin fact:** a detail that resembles an important one but doesn't change the best plan.
- **Optimization solver:** software that computes the mathematically best plan for a problem.

papers.title: BridgeKV: Large-Model Prefill and Small-Model Decoding for LLM Inference via KV Cache Translation
papers.tldr: A big model reads the prompt, a small model writes the reply, and a small translator between their memories recovers up to 80% of the quality gap at 3× the speed.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
BridgeKV lets a big AI model read your prompt and a small, cheap model write the answer, by translating the big model's "notes" on the prompt into a form the small model can use.

## Background you need
A chatbot answers in two phases. In **prefill**, it reads the whole prompt at once. In **decoding**, it writes the reply one word-piece at a time, which is slow because each step waits for the last. While reading, the model builds a **KV cache**: its short-term memory of the prompt, which every later step looks up. Big models understand prompts better but are slow and costly in the decoding phase.

## The problem
Decoding usually dominates the time and energy of a long answer. Using a big model for every generated token is expensive. Swapping in a small model saves money but loses quality, because the small model understands the prompt less well. Fine-tuning the small model helps, but a gap remains. Providers would love the big model's understanding at the small model's price.

## The idea
Picture a senior lawyer who reads a thick case file and writes detailed notes. A junior associate then drafts the letter, working from those notes. The junior doesn't need to be a genius to write well if the notes are good. The catch is that the two speak different shorthand. BridgeKV adds an interpreter that converts the senior's notes into the junior's shorthand.

## How it works
1. **Big model reads.** A large model handles the prefill phase and builds its KV cache for the prompt.
2. **Translate the memory.** A lightweight module converts that cache into the format a smaller model from the same family expects. Big and small models store memory in different shapes, so this step is needed.
3. **Small model writes.** The small model decodes the answer using the translated memory, as if it had read the prompt itself.
4. **Train only the bridge.** In the main training stage, both language models stay frozen (their weights don't change). Only the translator learns.
5. **Optional task tuning.** A second stage can add low-rank adapters (small add-on weights, a cheap way to fine-tune) to fit specific tasks.

## Results
The authors tested six big-to-small model pairs on five datasets, 30 settings in all. BridgeKV beat fine-tuned small models working alone in all 30. It closed up to 80% of the quality gap between the small model and running the big model for both phases. In practice, much of the big model's answer quality comes back without paying for big-model decoding.

On a single A40 GPU, pairing Llama-3.1-8B for reading with Llama-3.2-1B for writing ran 3.0 times faster than the 8B model alone. A reply that took 6 seconds would take about 2. In a simulated serving setup with a 70B reading model and a 1B writing model, the authors project requests up to 33.86 times faster and 27.5 times less energy.

## Why it matters
Serving costs are a major limit on how widely AI assistants can be offered. Splitting work this way could cut the price of long answers, especially where prompts are complex but replies are routine. Because the models stay frozen, providers can reuse model families they already run, adding only a small trained bridge.

## Caveats
The largest speed and energy gains come from a simulation, not a measured deployment. "Up to 80%" is the best case; some settings close less of the gap. The method needs big and small models from the same family. This summary is based on the paper's abstract, as the full text could not be retrieved, so details on translator design and failure cases are not covered here.

## Key terms
- **Prefill:** the phase where the model reads the whole prompt at once.
- **Decoding:** the phase where the model writes its reply one token at a time.
- **KV cache:** the model's stored memory of the text it has already read.
- **Frozen model:** a model whose weights are left unchanged during training.
- **Low-rank adapter:** a small set of extra weights used to tune a model cheaply.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems
papers.tldr: A study of 300 bug reports from libraries like FlashAttention and Triton finds about 60% of failures come from builds, compilers and environments, not the kernel code itself.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
The authors read through 300 real bug reports from seven popular GPU code libraries that power AI chatbots, and sorted out what actually goes wrong and why.

## Background you need
A GPU kernel is a small, highly tuned program that runs one math operation, like attention or matrix multiply, on a graphics chip. Large language models (LLMs) lean on shared kernel libraries such as FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS and bitsandbytes instead of writing these from scratch. A bug in one library can therefore hit many models and many kinds of hardware at once.

## The problem
When a kernel breaks, the damage varies. Sometimes the code won't build or install. Sometimes it crashes or hangs. Worst of all, it can quietly return wrong numbers. Earlier studies looked at bugs in AI frameworks and compilers, but nobody had looked closely at this kernel layer. So library developers and the teams deploying models had little evidence about where to focus testing.

## The idea
Think of a car recall analyst going through warranty claims. They don't redesign the engine. They read hundreds of repair tickets, sort them by symptom and cause, and tell engineers where the weak spots really are. This paper does that for GPU kernel libraries, using public GitHub issues as the repair tickets.

## How it works
1. **Collect reports.** The team pulled 9,099 issues from seven libraries: FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers and bitsandbytes.
2. **Filter to real failures.** They kept closed issues with failure-related titles and removed feature requests, questions, duplicates and reports with no evidence of a bug. That left 3,181 candidates.
3. **Sample fairly.** They picked 300 issues, with each library represented in proportion to its share of candidates.
4. **Label symptoms and causes.** Two authors labeled every issue separately, with one symptom (6 types) and one root cause (15 types in 3 groups). They agreed very closely, scoring 0.87 on a standard agreement measure where 1 means perfect.
5. **Study the fixes and tests.** They also looked at how bugs were fixed and what testing approaches the projects use.

## Results
The most common symptoms were deployment failures (27%), build failures (24%) and crashes (21%). Wrong results made up about 18%, slowdowns about 8%, and hangs 2%. More than half of the problems show up before the kernel ever runs on the GPU.

By cause, only about 40% came from the kernel code itself. About 60% came from the surrounding stack: the runtime environment (33%) and the compiler and build system (27%). The top single cause was software incompatibility, at 25%, such as mismatched library or driver versions. Next came the compiler transforming code incorrectly (15%) and build misconfiguration (12%).

The authors also found "implicit contracts." Fast kernels are specialized for certain tensor shapes, memory layouts and hardware limits. These rules are often unwritten. Break one, and even a supported operation can fail or return wrong answers. Current testing often misses small numeric errors in low-precision math and failures that only appear on specific GPUs.

## Why it matters
For anyone serving LLMs, the message is practical: testing the kernel alone is not enough. Checks need to cover builds, versions and the whole deployment setup. Library authors could write down shape and layout rules, or check them at runtime. Tool builders now have a map of which bug types deserve automated detectors.

## Caveats
The study covers only seven libraries, so results may not hold elsewhere. It sees only what people wrote in public issues, missing bugs fixed quietly. Labeling involves judgment, though two reviewers reduced this. Swapping out vague reports for clearer ones may tilt the sample toward well-documented bugs.

## Key terms
- **GPU kernel:** a tuned small program that runs one math step on a graphics chip.
- **Kernel library:** a shared collection of such kernels that many AI systems reuse.
- **Low precision:** storing numbers with fewer bits to save memory and time, at some accuracy risk.
- **Tensor shape and layout:** the dimensions of a block of numbers and how it sits in memory.
- **Implicit contract:** an unwritten rule the code assumes its inputs will follow.

papers.title: Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids (DASH): Latency-Agnostic Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models for Humanoid Manipulation
papers.tldr: Running a robot's slow AI brain and fast action head in parallel keeps control at 20 Hz regardless of model size, and lifts real humanoid pick-and-place success from 16/24 to 23/24.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
DASH lets a humanoid robot use a big, smart AI "brain" without slowing down its hands, by letting the slow thinking part and the fast moving part run at the same time instead of taking turns.

## Background you need
A vision-language-action model (VLA) is an AI that looks at camera images, reads an instruction like "put the cup in the bin," and outputs motor commands. Most VLAs have two parts: a large backbone (a vision-language model that understands the scene and words) and an action head (a smaller network that turns that understanding into movements). The control rate is how many times per second the robot gets a fresh command, measured in hertz (Hz).

## The problem
In today's usual setup, the robot waits for the whole model to finish before it moves. The big backbone is the slow step. So a bigger, smarter backbone means the robot acts on older and older camera images. In the paper's simulator, the control rate falls from 9.7 Hz with a 0.8-billion-parameter backbone to just 4.1 Hz with an 8-billion one. For a robot hand grabbing objects, acting on a picture that is a quarter-second old makes motions jerky and less reliable. Builders face an awkward trade: smarter or more reactive, but not both.

## The idea
Think of a rally car with a navigator and a driver. The navigator reads the map and calls out turns now and then. The driver keeps steering every instant using their own eyes. The driver never stops the car to wait for the next call. DASH works the same way: the big model is the navigator, and the action head is the driver with its own fresh view of the road.

## How it works
1. **Split into two systems.** The slow vision-language model ("System 2") and the fast action head ("System 1") run as separate processes. They pass messages through a channel where each side just reads the latest available message, so nobody blocks.
2. **Share cached understanding.** The backbone (a Qwen3-VL model) publishes its internal signals from four depths of its network. The action head reuses these cached signals until a newer batch arrives.
3. **Give the fast part its own eyes.** The action head has its own small image encoder (a ResNet, a classic image network). It looks at the current camera frame every cycle, so its view is always fresh even when the backbone's view is stale.
4. **Train for staleness on purpose.** During training, the backbone is shown an older frame, picked at random up to the delay seen on real hardware. The action head sees the current frame. This "desynchronized training" teaches the policy to cope with out-of-date context. The backbone stays frozen; only the action head and its encoder are trained.
5. **Smooth the handoffs.** The action head predicts short sequences of moves ("chunks"). An adaptive aggregator lines up overlapping chunks using the measured timing, so motions don't drift or stutter.

## Results
In a modified RoboTwin simulator (50 tasks, where thinking time counts against the robot), DASH held a steady 20 Hz at every backbone size. That is 2.1 to 4.9 times faster than the wait-for-everything baseline. Success was also higher at every size: for example 69.5% versus 63.6% with a 4-billion-parameter backbone, and 65.9% versus 62.7% at 8 billion. Running the split setup without the staleness training did worse, showing that training step matters. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH succeeded in 23 of 24 pick-and-place trials, against 16 of 24 for the standard pipeline.

## Why it matters
Robot teams want larger models because they understand instructions and scenes better. DASH removes much of the speed penalty for going bigger. That could let home or factory humanoids run stronger backbones on the same hardware while staying responsive.

## Caveats
The real-robot test is small: 24 trials on one pick-and-place task. Gains in simulation are a few percentage points, not dramatic. Timing was measured on a single consumer GPU, and the simulated delays may not match every real deployment. Because the backbone is frozen, the system cannot tune its scene understanding to a new task.

## Key terms
- **VLA (vision-language-action model):** an AI that turns images plus instructions into robot motions.
- **Backbone:** the large, general model that understands what it sees and reads.
- **Action head:** the smaller network that produces the actual motor commands.
- **Control rate:** how many fresh commands per second the robot receives.
- **Action chunk:** a short planned sequence of moves predicted in one go.
- **Frozen:** a part of the model whose weights are not changed during training.
